one_liner: Tiny C LZ77 compressor with gamma-coded lengths/offsets; at -6 it matches zlib -9's ratio with about 2x faster compression.
what_it_does: Compresses and decompresses whole in-memory buffers with a raw block format (no header, no stored length, no checksum). The API is a handful of C functions: blz_pack / blz_pack_level(src, dst, size, workmem, level 1-10), blz_depack(src, dst, depacked_size) and a bounds-checked blz_depack_safe(src, src_size, dst, depacked_size). It is not zlib-compatible: the caller supplies the work buffer and must record the uncompressed size; framing, block splitting and checksums are left to the application (the blzpack example adds a 24-byte block header and 1 MiB blocks).
how_it_is_fast: LZSS-style matching with an Elias-gamma (gamma2) universal code for lengths and offsets and 16-bit tag words for literal/match flags, so there is no Huffman stage to build or decode. Levels pick the match finder: a single-entry hash table (level 1), lazy matching (2), hash buckets (3-4), a backwards dynamic-programming parse with left-extension of matches (5-7) and a binary-tree optimal parse (8-10). The decoder uses a 256-entry lookup table to read up to 8 bits of gamma code at a time; decode stays around 300-400 MB/s because the bit-level format is serial.
when_to_use: Code size of the decompressor matters: blz_depack is 61 lines of C, which the README says fits in 103 bytes of x86 machine code (boot loaders, executable packers, firmware, demos).
Compress-once, decompress-many assets where you want a ratio near zlib -9 (31.71% vs 31.92% on Silesia) without carrying zlib's inflate.
Small embedded or C89 targets that need a permissively licensed (Zlib) single-file compressor with no dependencies and caller-provided memory.
Buffers whose full size is known up front, since the format has no window limit and matches can reach back across the whole buffer.
when_not_to_use: Throughput-sensitive code on desktop or server CPUs: libdeflate 1.26 -6 in the same lzbench 2.4 run gives 31.85% at 82.1 MB/s compress and 820 MB/s decompress versus brieflz -6 at 31.71%, 22.8 and 328 MB/s, and zstd beats both.
Anything that needs the deflate/gzip/zlib format, streaming, or interoperability with other tools; BriefLZ has its own raw format with no streaming API.
Untrusted input to the plain decoder: blz_depack does no bounds checking, so use blz_depack_safe for data you did not produce.

Level 10 (--optimal) or other high levels on attacker-controlled or highly repetitive data: open issue #12 reports about 1000x slowdowns on runs of a single byte, and issue #11 reports unpredictable speed.

Very large buffers: workmem grows with input (levels 5-7 need about 3x src_size words, levels 8-10 about 5x src_size words plus the hash table), and sizes are unsigned long, which is 32-bit on 64-bit Windows.

integration.form: static lib | shared lib | source-drop (src/brieflz.c, src/depack.c or src/depacks.c, include/brieflz.h)
integration.min_toolchain: ANSI C (C89); CMake 2.8.11+ for the provided build
integration.platforms: any; 16-bit targets need BLZ_HASH_BITS and the block size lowered
integration.thread_safety: not documented; functions keep no global state and all scratch is in the caller's workmem, so separate workmem buffers per thread should be safe (inferred from source)

gotchas: The compressed stream does not store the original size; you must keep it yourself and pass it to blz_depack.
dst must be at least blz_max_packed_size(n) = n + n/8 + 64 bytes, and workmem must be blz_workmem_size_level(n, level) bytes, which differs by level.
The README notes its benchmark 'is not entirely fair because BriefLZ has no window size limit'; with blzpack's 1 MiB blocks, real ratios are lower than whole-file numbers.
Interfaces use unsigned long for sizes (C89); the blzpack example misreports totals above 4 GiB where unsigned long is 32-bit (issue #1, wontfix).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick BriefLZ over zlib, libdeflate or zstd only when decoder footprint and a tiny, dependency-free, Zlib-licensed codebase matter more than speed; for raw speed LZ4 or libdeflate win, and for ratio-per-second zstd wins. Against FastLZ and LZ4 it trades speed for ratio (31.71% at -6 vs about 47-49%).
verified_claims_summary: In lzbench 2.4 (gcc 15.2.0 release binary, one thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.2 GHz with turbo off, silesia.tar), brieflz 1.3.0 -6 compresses at 22.8 MB/s and decompresses at 328 MB/s to 31.71%, against zlib 1.3.2 -9 at 11.3 and 318 MB/s to 31.92%: about 2x faster compression and similar decompression at a slightly better ratio; versus zlib -6 it compresses slower (22.8 vs 26.8 MB/s). The README's own 2020 table on a Core i5-4570 shows 17 vs 11 MB/s and 400 vs 320 MB/s against zlib 1.2.11 -9.
status_note: Version 1.3.0 (2020) with only CI updates since (last commit 2024-02-02) and two open performance issues unanswered; it is small, Zlib-licensed and easy to vendor, so staleness matters little for a frozen format.
